title: OSA: Echocardiography Video Segmentation via Orthogonalized State Update and Anatomical Prior-aware Feature Enhancement — CVPR 2026
description: OSA: Echocardiography Video Segmentation via Orthogonalized State Update and Anatomical Prior-aware Feature Enhancement
publicationTitle: OSA: Echocardiography Video Segmentation via Orthogonalized State Update and Anatomical Prior-aware Feature Enhancement
venueFull: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 2026
fig1Caption: Overview of the proposed OSA framework. Top: unconstrained linear recurrent models suffer from rank collapse under severe speckle noise. Middle: our OSU mechanism constrains state evolution on the Stiefel manifold, preventing singular value decay. Bottom: the APFE module decouples anatomical structures from speckle noise via physics-driven decomposition, providing noise-resilient cues for temporal tracking.
abstractP1: Accurate and temporally consistent segmentation of the left ventricle from echocardiography videos is essential for estimating the ejection fraction and assessing cardiac function. However, modeling spatiotemporal dynamics remains difficult due to severe speckle noise and rapid non-rigid deformations.
abstractP2: Existing linear recurrent models offer efficient in-context associative recall for temporal tracking, but rely on unconstrained state updates, which cause progressive singular value decay in the state matrix—a phenomenon known as rank collapse—resulting in anatomical details being overwhelmed by noise.
abstractP3: To address this, we propose OSA, a framework that constrains the state evolution on the Stiefel manifold. We introduce the Orthogonalized State Update (OSU) mechanism, which formulates memory evolution as Euclidean projected gradient descent on the Stiefel manifold to prevent rank collapse and maintain stable temporal transitions.
abstractP4: Furthermore, an Anatomical Prior-aware Feature Enhancement module explicitly separates anatomical structures from speckle noise through a physics-driven process, providing the temporal tracker with noise-resilient structural cues. Comprehensive experiments on the CAMUS and EchoNet-Dynamic datasets show that OSA achieves state-of-the-art segmentation accuracy and temporal stability, while maintaining real-time inference efficiency for clinical deployment.
motivationDesc: Echocardiography video segmentation faces severe challenges from speckle noise, low contrast, rapid non-rigid cardiac deformation, and sparse clinical annotations. Existing methods struggle to jointly satisfy accuracy, temporal consistency, and real-time efficiency.
fig2Caption: Challenges in echocardiography video segmentation. (a) Severe speckle noise obscures anatomical boundaries. (b) Low contrast between myocardium and blood pool. (c) Rapid non-rigid deformation between systole and diastole. (d) Depth-dependent acoustic attenuation. (e) Sparse annotations (ED/ES only). (f) Real-time clinical requirements.
methodOsuDesc: OSU constrains the memory evolution to the Stiefel manifold via an orthogonalized update. By enforcing strict orthogonality, the Frobenius norm of the state remains constant, preventing singular value decay and rank collapse. A parameterized high-order Newton-Schulz iteration achieves efficient projection without explicit SVD, reducing computational cost from O(Cv Ck^2) to a fixed number of matrix multiplications.
methodApfeDesc: APFE reformulates spatial feature extraction as a physics-driven decoupling process. It decomposes the feature map into a low-frequency acoustic bias field and high-frequency structural residuals via large-kernel average pooling. Dual Conv-BN-ReLU pathways separately handle structural geometry and region-level semantics, fused via an adaptive gating mechanism. This provides noise-resilient structural anchors for the temporal tracker.
fig3Caption: Architecture of the Orthogonalized State Update (OSU) mechanism. Left: standard Euclidean recurrence allows the state to deviate from the manifold, causing rank collapse. Right: OSU explicitly projects the unconstrained state back onto the Stiefel manifold, preserving orthogonality and preventing singular value decay.
apfeCaption: Architecture of the Anatomical Prior-aware Feature Enhancement (APFE) module. A large-kernel average pooling decomposes the feature map into a low-frequency acoustic bias field and high-frequency structural residuals. Dual Conv-BN-ReLU pathways separately process structural geometry and region-level semantics, fused via an adaptive gating mechanism to provide noise-resilient structural anchors for temporal tracking.
resultsDesc: OSA achieves state-of-the-art performance on CAMUS and EchoNet-Dynamic datasets, with 94.82 mDice and 35 fps real-time inference.
fig4Caption: Qualitative segmentation results on CAMUS and EchoNet-Dynamic. OSA consistently yields more accurate contours across varying imaging qualities, acoustic shadowing, and ambiguous boundaries.

poster.quantitativeResultsBody: SOTA on CAMUS & EchoNet-Dynamic in terms of mDice and mHD95. OSA achieves 94.82% mDice and competitive mHD95 performance, reflecting superior boundary precision crucial for clinical measurement. Inference runs at 35 fps, enabling real-time clinical deployment.

poster.qualitativeComparisonBody: OSA shows superior boundary adherence and fewer false positives in speckle-dense regions. Compared to state-of-the-art methods such as SAMed-2 and EchoVim, OSA maintains consistent contour tracking across the full cardiac cycle even under severe acoustic shadowing and low-contrast apical views.

interactive.title: See the idea, not just the diagram
interactive.intro: Follow a frame through OSA: first separate complementary feature cues, then stabilize the evolving memory. Move the controls to explore the underlying mathematics.
interactive.apfeIntro: A local average captures slow intensity variation. Positive and negative deviations retain complementary contrasts around that local field.
interactive.apfeEquationAlt: Input equals local mean plus positive residual minus negative residual
interactive.apfeInputAlt: Synthetic feature field with left-ventricle-like geometry and adjustable noise
interactive.apfePositiveAlt: Positive part of the difference between input and local average
interactive.apfeNegativeAlt: Negative part of the difference between input and local average
interactive.apfeLesson: The decomposition is algebraically exact, but it does not perfectly isolate anatomy: high-frequency speckle can remain in both residuals. In the real network, learned convolutions and an adaptive gate fuse these channels.
interactive.osuIntro: Both sides receive the same sequence of gated updates. Only the right side projects each intermediate state back to an orthogonal basis.
interactive.osuEquationAlt: The state transpose times the state equals the identity matrix under ideal orthogonality
interactive.osuBaselineAlt: Two state column vectors without orthogonalization, updated as the frame slider changes
interactive.osuProposedAlt: Two state column vectors with ideal 2D polar projection, updated as the frame slider changes
interactive.osuLesson: This toy example uses the paper's gated recurrence (Eq. 1) and an ideal 2D polar projection. Actual OSU uses a scaled, finite-step Newton–Schulz approximation; these bars are computed from toy matrices, not measured model states.
interactive.disclaimer: Educational illustrations, not patient scans, network predictions, or reported experimental trajectories. Residual colors are visually amplified for clarity.

study.entryTitle: One frame. Two kinds of information.
study.entryDesc: A visual walkthrough of a frame's spatial features and the memory carried across time. Select any module to see its role.
study.scanAlt: Generated ultrasound-like texture and animated illustrative left-ventricle contour, not a patient scan or OSA model output
study.scanFallback: A synthetic moving visualization is available when scripting is enabled.
study.scanNote: Generated geometry and texture, not medical footage, ground truth or a measured segmentation result.
study.flowAlt: Backbone features flow to APFE, then OSU and decoder; the previous OSU state feeds the next time step.
study.backboneDesc: The ResNet-50 backbone turns each ultrasound frame into feature maps. A feature map is a grid of numerical measurements, not the original pixels.
study.apfeDesc: APFE decomposes each feature into a local mean and positive/negative contrasts. Learned convolution branches and an adaptive gate combine the cues; this is not perfect speckle removal.
study.osuDesc: OSU updates a matrix state with the new frame, then approximately projects it toward orthogonal columns. The state also flows from one time step to the next.
study.decoderDesc: The decoder turns the tracked features into a segmentation. The animation here is a teaching example, not an actual decoder prediction.
study.inspectorHint: Follow the arrows to see the sequence; the lower loop shows the state returning from the previous frame.
study.whyTitle: A hard-to-see boundary should not become an unstable memory.
study.whyDesc: Echocardiograms change shape rapidly and contain severe speckle. OSA tackles the spatial ambiguity with APFE and the temporal memory problem with OSU.
study.difficulty1Desc: The ventricle changes appearance throughout the cardiac cycle.
study.difficulty2Desc: Speckle and low contrast can obscure its boundary.
study.difficulty3Desc: Unconstrained recurrent state directions may lose independence over time.
study.conceptTitle: What does losing a direction actually mean?
study.conceptIntro: Move the angle between two unit vectors. The geometry below explains two terms you will encounter in OSU without requiring linear algebra first.
study.vectorAlt: Two unit arrows with an adjustable angle, demonstrating linear independence
study.sigmaShort: How much a direction is squeezed
study.angleNeutral: The arrows point in different directions, but the matrix is not perfectly balanced.
study.angleOrthogonal: Perpendicular directions are easy to distinguish: the minimum singular value is 1 and the condition number is 1.
study.angleNear: Nearly aligned directions become difficult to distinguish. Watch the smallest singular value fall and the condition number rise.
study.sigmaExplanation: Imagine drawing a circle on a rubber sheet and stretching it with a matrix. The circle becomes an ellipse. Singular values are how much its longest and shortest axes were stretched. The smallest tells us whether a direction has nearly disappeared.
study.conditionExplanation: Divide the biggest stretch by the smallest. A value of 1 means equally strong directions; a very large number means some directions are much harder to recover. When the smallest singular value is zero, the condition number is infinite.
study.projectionQuestion: How does this connect to OSU?
study.projectionExplanation: An ideal orthogonal state has perpendicular unit columns, so its singular values are all 1. The actual paper uses a finite-step Newton–Schulz approximation after state updates—not the perfect 2D correction shown here.
study.geometryDisclaimer: The arrows and numbers are an exact calculation on an invented 2×2 matrix. They do not represent OSA measurements or a clinical result.
